name: Cerridwen
title: Keeper of the Cauldron of Inspiration
represents: Cerridwen is the brewer of awen, the flowing poetic and prophetic inspiration of Welsh tradition. She rules the cauldron as a vessel of knowledge, rebirth and initiation: the long patient brewing, the terrible pursuit, and the swallowing that ends in a new birth. She embodies transformation that is earned rather than given, and the fierce mother-wisdom that both destroys and remakes. Modern witches see her as a goddess of the dark moon, of shapeshifting, of herbcraft, and of the creative fire of poets and seers.
description:
Cerridwen's great tale survives in the Hanes Taliesin (the Tale of Taliesin), written down most fully by Elis Gruffydd in the mid-16th century, though drawing on much older bardic material. Living by Llyn Tegid (Bala Lake) with her husband Tegid Foel, she had a son, Morfran, so ill-favoured that she resolved to brew him a cauldron of wisdom. For a year and a day the boy Gwion Bach stirred it, until three scalding drops leapt onto his thumb; he sucked it and gained all knowledge, and the rest of the brew became poison and the cauldron split.

Cerridwen pursued him through a cycle of shapeshifting: he became a hare and she a greyhound, he a fish and she an otter, he a bird and she a hawk, until he became a grain of wheat and she a black hen who swallowed him. Nine months later she bore him, could not bring herself to kill so beautiful a child, and set him adrift in a leather bag. He was found at a weir by Elffin and named Taliesin, 'radiant brow', the greatest of the poets. Poems in the medieval Book of Taliesin also refer to the 'cauldron of Ceridwen' as the source of bardic inspiration.

Honesty matters here: there is no clear evidence of a pre-Christian cult of Cerridwen, no temples or inscriptions; medieval texts present her as a powerful enchantress, and some scholars think the goddess reading grew from the poets' use of her cauldron as a metaphor for awen. Since the 19th-century Celtic revival, and especially in Wicca and Druidry from the mid-20th century onward, she has been embraced as a Crone goddess, Lady of the Cauldron and patron of initiates. That modern devotion is living and meaningful, but it is a modern growth from a medieval root.
sacredDays: Samhain and the dark half of the year; modern practice favours the dark and waning moon, and any long work of study or brewing begun on a new moon and carried for a year and a day.
howToInvoke: Set a small cauldron or iron pot at the centre of a dark cloth, with a black or deep purple candle beside it and a bowl of grain or barley. Pour a little water, mead or a gentle herbal brew into the cauldron. Sit or kneel close to it, gaze into the liquid by candlelight, and speak to her slowly, as to an exacting teacher. Ask for inspiration or the courage to change, never for shortcuts. Afterwards stir the brew sunwise three times (for the three drops), pour it onto the earth with thanks, snuff the candle and record whatever words or images came to you. Keep any promise you make to her.
invocation:
Cerridwen, Mother of the brimming pot,
Lady of the lake and of the year-long fire,
I come to the rim of your cauldron with an open hand.
Stir in me the awen, the three bright drops,
that what I was may melt, and what I am may wake.
Hound and hare, otter and fish, hawk and wren,
hen and the hidden grain, I run, I change, I am reborn.
Teach me patience at the fire and courage in the chase.
Cerridwen, keeper of the brew, I honour you.
offerings: a small cauldron of homemade herbal brew or broth
mead or dark ale poured onto the earth
bread baked by your own hand
a poem or song you wrote yourself
a candle kept burning through a long study session
a promise of study kept for a year and a day
avoid: Don't approach her for quick fixes or treat the cauldron as a vending machine; she is famously exacting. Never drink from or offer any toxic herb brew, and don't leave candles or cauldron fires unattended.
bestTime: Samhain through midwinter (Oct–Dec), the dark half of the year; also any season of study, initiation or major life change
caution: Welsh tradition and Welsh-language culture are living; honour the source texts and their Welsh context rather than flattening her into a generic crone. Much of her goddess role is modern interpretation, which is fine to practise as long as it isn't presented as ancient fact. Work at the cauldron is about real transformation and can stir up difficult feelings; go gently.

name: Brigid
title: Lady of the Sacred Flame, Well and Forge
represents: Brigid is the bright one of the hearth fire, the holy well and the smith's forge: she rules poetry and inspiration, healing and midwifery, and craft and metalwork. She stands at the threshold of spring, when lambs are born and ewes give milk. As goddess and saint woven together she is protector of home, livestock, mothers and children, and a keeper of flame for anyone who must make, mend or create.
description:
The 9th-10th century Sanas Cormaic (Cormac's Glossary) describes Brigit as a poetess and daughter of the Dagda, 'a goddess whom poets adored', and says she had two sisters of the same name: Brigit the physician and Brigit the smith, so that all Irish goddesses were called Brigit. In the mythological tradition she is linked with the Tuatha Dé Danann, and in Cath Maige Tuired she is said to have raised the first keening in Ireland when her son Ruadán was killed. Some scholars connect her with the British goddess Brigantia, though the link is debated.

St Brigid of Kildare (traditionally c. 451-525) is one of Ireland's patron saints, and her feast on 1 February coincides with Imbolc, the ancient start of spring. Gerald of Wales recorded in the 12th century that nuns at Kildare kept a perpetual fire, hedged so no man could enter, tended by nineteen sisters with Brigid herself tending it on the twentieth night. Whether the saint 'absorbed' an earlier goddess is debated: the overlap of name, feast, fire and functions is striking, but the hagiography is a Christian tradition in its own right and deserves respect as such.

Folk customs of Lá Fhéile Bríde are well documented and still practised: weaving rush Brigid's crosses, making a Brídeóg doll carried from house to house, leaving out the brat Bríde (a cloth or ribbon for her to bless overnight), and visiting her holy wells. The Kildare flame was relit in 1993 by the Brigidine Sisters and burns at Solas Bhríde. Modern pagans, Druids and Wiccans honour Brigid as a Triple Goddess of fire, well and forge at Imbolc, often alongside Christians who honour the saint.
sacredDays: Imbolc / Lá Fhéile Bríde (1 February, eve on 31 January); Brigid's Day is now a public holiday in Ireland. Modern devotees tend her flame on a 20-day cycle like the Kildare nuns.
howToInvoke: Cleanse your hearth or a small table and set a white or red candle in a fireproof dish beside a bowl of water (well water if you have it). Add a Brigid's cross, a sprig of greenery, and a cup of milk. Light the candle with intent, saying her name three times, and ask her blessing on your home, your health or your creative work. Lay a ribbon or cloth outside on Imbolc Eve for the brat Bríde and bring it in the next morning to use as a healing charm. Thank her, pour the milk outside, and either let the candle burn safely or snuff it with a promise to rekindle it.
offerings: a Brigid's cross woven by hand
a candle kept burning safely in her honour
clean water or water from a holy well
a poem, song or piece of craftwork
early spring flowers such as snowdrops or dandelions
acts of service: caring for the sick, mothers, children or animals
avoid: Don't neglect her flame if you promise to tend it, and never leave candles unattended. Avoid mocking or dismissing the Christian saint; many devotees, and Ireland itself, honour both.
bestTime: Imbolc (31 Jan–2 Feb) and late winter into early spring; also whenever beginning a creative project or seeking healing
caution: St Brigid is a living Catholic and Anglican saint and Brigid is a national symbol in Ireland; holy wells are often active pilgrimage sites, so visit respectfully and leave no litter. Be clear in your own practice about where the documented goddess, the saint and modern neopagan interpretation meet.

name: The Morrígan
title: The Great Queen of Battle and Prophecy
represents: The Morrígan rules battle, fate, prophecy and sovereignty over the land. She appears before conflict washing the armour of those about to die, shrieks over the field as a crow, and speaks prophecy in verse. She is not simply a death-goddess: she incites, warns and grants victory, and she is bound to the land's protection and fertility. Modern devotees approach her as a goddess of personal power, boundaries, justice and facing what must be faced.
description:
The Morrígan appears across medieval Irish literature. In Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired) she meets the Dagda at Samhain as she stands astride the river Unshin washing, and after their union promises aid against the Fomorians; at the battle's end she proclaims a famous prophecy of peace and then a darker prophecy of the world's ending. In the Ulster Cycle, especially the Táin Bó Cúailnge and Táin Bó Regamna, she offers herself to Cú Chulainn, is refused, and harries him in the shapes of an eel, a she-wolf and a heifer; at his death a crow settles on his shoulder.

She is often part of a trio of sisters, the daughters of Ernmas, variously named Badb, Macha and the Morrígan (whose personal name is sometimes given as Anand), or with Nemain. The name is usually read as 'Great Queen' (mór-ríoghain), though 'Phantom Queen' (from mor, 'terror' or 'phantom') is also argued. The 'washer at the ford', a figure who washes the clothes of those soon to die, is connected with her and with later banshee lore. The Dá Chích na Morrígna ('Paps of the Morrígan') in Co. Meath are named after her.

We have no surviving description of a formal cult, so details of ancient worship are unknown. The popular image of her as a dark Triple Goddess of sex and death largely grew in the 20th century; modern devotional polytheists, Celtic reconstructionists and witches have since built a vibrant practice around her, emphasising sovereignty, warriorship, protection of the vulnerable and service to the land.
sacredDays: Samhain above all (her meeting with the Dagda); modern practice also honours her at times of struggle, before contests or legal battles, and on Tuesdays (Mars-day).
howToInvoke: Prepare a dark altar with a black and a red candle, a bowl of water (for the ford), a feather and a stone or blade. Stand rather than kneel, if you can, and speak plainly and honestly; she is known for valuing courage and directness. State what you are prepared to do, not just what you want. Pour an offering of whiskey, red wine or water and listen in silence; note crows, dreams or words that come. Close by thanking her, pouring the offering outside at a tree or stream, and following through on any commitment.
invocation:
Great Queen, Phantom Queen, washer at the ford,
crow upon the shoulder, word upon the sword,
I stand before you with my spine made straight,
to name my battle and to meet my fate.
Grant me sight to see the coming tide,
strength to hold the line, and courage at my side.
Sovereign of the land, I keep my word to you:
what I vow tonight, I swear that I will do.
offerings: whiskey, red wine or dark mead
fresh water poured at a stream or ford
dark rye bread, oatcakes or barley cakes
a naturally shed crow feather returned to the land
a vow of discipline kept (training, study, a boundary held)
acts of service for veterans, survivors or protectors of the vulnerable
litter-picking or tending a battlefield, cairn or wild place
a spoken poem in her honour
avoid: Don't make promises to her you won't keep, and don't approach her casually or to curse in petty spite. Never offer blood or harm any creature; don't take feathers from protected birds or disturb nests.
bestTime: Samhain (31 Oct–1 Nov) and the dark half of the year; also any time of struggle, conflict or reclaiming personal sovereignty
caution: Many devotees describe her as intense and demanding; approach with genuine respect and without fantasy of control. Irish culture and its literature are living heritage: read the sources rather than relying on modern blogs, and avoid presenting the modern triple-goddess image as ancient fact.

name: Cernunnos
title: The Horned Lord of Beasts and Wild Places
represents: Cernunnos is the antlered god who sits cross-legged among animals, wearing or holding a torc: lord of beasts, of wild nature, of the cycle of growth and death, and possibly of wealth and the underworld. To modern witches he is the Horned God himself, the wild consort of the Goddess, the stag-king of the forest, and a patron of fertility, abundance, and the untamed body and spirit.
description:
The name Cernunnos is directly attested only once: on the Pillar of the Boatmen (Pilier des Nautes), a monument dedicated by the guild of Parisii boatmen during the reign of Tiberius (c. 14-37 CE) and found in 1710 beneath Notre-Dame de Paris. One block shows an older man with stag's antlers, each hung with a torc, above a label reading '[C]ERNUNNOS' (the first letter is damaged). A related name, 'Carnonos', appears on inscriptions from southern Gaul, and the name is usually taken to mean 'horned one'.

The most famous image associated with him, the antlered figure on the Gundestrup cauldron (a silver vessel found in a Danish bog in 1891, probably made around 150-1 BCE), is not labelled; it shows a seated antlered man holding a torc and a ram-horned serpent, surrounded by a stag and other beasts. Scholars apply the name Cernunnos to this and to many other antlered or cross-legged figures from Gaul (some with coins or bags of grain pouring from them), but this is a modern convention of identification. No myths about him survive.

The 'Horned God' of modern Wicca, shaped by Margaret Murray's (now discredited) witch-cult theory and by Gerald Gardner from the 1950s, draws heavily on Cernunnos along with Pan and Herne the Hunter. Today he is one of the most beloved deities in neopagan practice, celebrated especially at Beltane and Samhain. That rich modern devotion is real, but it rests on a very small ancient base: one inscription, a scatter of images, and much inspired imagination.
sacredDays: Beltane (1 May) and Samhain (31 Oct) in modern practice; the autumn rut and the shedding of antlers in late winter are natural markers of his year.
howToInvoke: Go outdoors to a woodland edge if you can, or make a woodland altar of moss, stones, a shed antler or pine cones, and a green or brown candle. Sit cross-legged on the ground as he does in his images, breathe slowly and feel your weight sink into the earth. Call him by name, drumming or clapping a heartbeat rhythm. Ask for vitality, grounding, abundance or a deeper bond with wild things. Leave a natural, biodegradable offering, thank him, and before you leave pick up any litter you find as an act of devotion.
invocation:
Horned One of the greenwood deep,
Lord of the stag and the serpent's sleep,
torc of gold in your open hand,
heartbeat of the wild and wandering land,
Cernunnos, rise from root and stone;
teach my body it is not alone.
In rut and rest, in life and death,
I share with all that lives one breath.
offerings: fresh water or ale poured on the earth
a coin (left where it won't harm wildlife, or given to charity)
tree planting or wildlife conservation work
avoid: Never harm animals in his name or take antlers from living creatures; use only naturally shed antlers or images. Don't leave plastic, glitter or non-biodegradable offerings in the wild.
bestTime: Beltane (May) and Samhain (Oct–Nov); also late autumn during the deer rut
caution: Be honest that almost all lore about him is modern; don't present Wiccan Horned God mythology as ancient Gaulish religion. Respect wild places and wildlife laws when gathering items.

name: Rhiannon
title: The Great Queen of the White Mare
represents: Rhiannon is the radiant otherworld woman who rides an unhurried white horse no one can catch, chooses her own husband, and endures a cruel false accusation with dignity. She represents sovereignty and choice, patience and endurance through injustice, the bond of mother and child, and the songs of her birds that wake the dead and lull the living to sleep. Modern witches call on her for justice, emotional healing, dream work and courage in suffering.
description:
Rhiannon appears in the First and Third Branches of the Mabinogi (medieval Welsh tales preserved in the White Book of Rhydderch and Red Book of Hergest, c. 14th century, with material much older). In the First Branch, Pwyll, lord of Dyfed, sits on the mound of Gorsedd Arberth and sees her ride past on a pale horse; however fast his riders go they cannot catch her, until Pwyll simply calls out and she stops. She has chosen him over another suitor, and with wit and a magic bag she helps him win her hand.

When their infant son vanishes, her terrified maids smear her with a puppy's blood and accuse her of killing him. As penance she must sit by the horse-block at the gate for seven years, offering to carry visitors on her back like a horse. The boy is found and raised by Teyrnon, named Pryderi ('care' or 'worry'), and returned; Rhiannon is vindicated. In the Third Branch, married to Manawydan, she is trapped by enchantment and made to wear the collars of asses until he wins her freedom. The 'Birds of Rhiannon', whose song wakes the dead and lulls the living, appear in the Second Branch and in Culhwch and Olwen.

The Mabinogi never calls her a goddess. Scholars have long suggested her name derives from a Brythonic *Rīgantonā, 'great queen', and compared her with the Gaulish horse goddess Epona, but these links are theoretical. Modern pagans honour her as a goddess of horses, sovereignty, dreams and the Otherworld, and as a patron of those who are wrongly accused.
items: a mounting block or threshold stone
animals: badger (from the 'badger in the bag' game)
sacredDays: Beltane (May Eve, when Teyrnon's foal and Pryderi appear); modern practice also honours her on Mondays and nights of the full moon.
howToInvoke: Set a white candle, a horseshoe or horse figurine, a bowl of apples and a small bell on a white or pale green cloth. Ring the bell three times as birdsong, and speak her name softly. She comes to those who ask, not those who chase: be patient and simply call. Tell her of the burden you carry or the justice you seek, and ask for dignity and endurance. Listen for music or birdsong in dreams. Close with thanks, leave the apples for horses or wildlife, and ring the bell once more.
invocation:
Rhiannon of the white mare's gentle pace,
who cannot be caught yet comes when called with grace,
Queen who sat seven years beside the gate
and bore the false word with an unbowed weight,
sing me your birds to soothe the grieving heart,
to wake what sleeps and let the sorrow part.
Lady of the mound, I call and do not chase:
ride to me now, and lend me your strength and grace.
offerings: apples, oats or carrots (shared with horses if you know any)
a song or the sound of bells
donations to horse rescue or care for horses
speaking up for someone wrongly accused
avoid: Don't try to force or bargain hard with her; her story teaches that she comes to those who ask with courtesy. Never mistreat horses or animals, or offer anything harmful to wildlife.
bestTime: Beltane through midsummer (May–Jun), and any time you face injustice or false accusation
caution: Her goddess status is a scholarly and modern interpretation; the Welsh texts present her as a noble otherworld queen. Honour Welsh-language culture and the Mabinogi as literature in their own right.

name: Arianrhod
title: Lady of the Silver Wheel
represents: Arianrhod, 'silver wheel' or 'silver round', is a proud and independent lady of the Fourth Branch who lays fates upon her son and refuses to be shamed or controlled. In modern practice she is a goddess of the moon and stars, the turning wheel of time and fate, initiation, reincarnation and the sovereign self, ruling from her sea-girt tower Caer Arianrhod, often identified with the Corona Borealis.
description:
Arianrhod appears in Math fab Mathonwy, the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi. She is daughter of Dôn and sister of Gwydion. When Math needs a new virgin footholder, Arianrhod steps over his magic wand to prove her maidenhood and immediately gives birth to two children: Dylan, who runs to the sea and becomes a sea-creature, and a small 'thing' that Gwydion snatches and raises. Humiliated, she lays three tynghedau (destinies or prohibitions) on the boy: he shall have no name unless she gives it, bear no arms unless she arms him, and have no wife of any human race.

Gwydion tricks her twice in disguise into naming the boy Lleu Llaw Gyffes ('the fair one of the skilful hand') and arming him, and then he and Math make Blodeuwedd from flowers as his wife. Arianrhod's court, Caer Arianrhod, is said to lie off the coast near Dinas Dinlle in Gwynedd, where a rock reef visible at low tide carries the name; in later Welsh tradition the name was also given to the constellation Corona Borealis. The Welsh Triads list her among the three fair maidens of Britain.

The Mabinogi does not call her a goddess, and her lunar and stellar associations are mostly the work of 20th-century writers, especially Robert Graves and later Wiccan authors, who made her a moon goddess and keeper of the silver wheel of reincarnation. Modern witches love her as a sovereign woman who answers to no one, and as a patron of star magic, fate work and lunar ritual; these are inspired modern readings.
sacredDays: Full moons and clear starry nights; modern practice links her to the winter solstice and the turning of the year's wheel.
howToInvoke: On a clear night go outside or sit by a window where you can see the moon or stars. Place a silver or white candle on a round mirror, ringed with seashells or silver objects, and if possible locate the Corona Borealis (high in summer evenings for northern-hemisphere viewers). Turn slowly sunwise once as the wheel turns, then stand still and address her as an equal and a sovereign. Ask for clarity about your path or the strength to keep your independence. Thank her, cover the mirror and journal any dreams that night.
invocation:
Arianrhod of the silver wheel,
queen of the tower the tides reveal,
spinner of stars and keeper of fate,
you who will bow to no one's weight,
turn your bright circle over me,
show me the path I was meant to be.
Lady of the Northern Crown,
let your silver light shine down.
offerings: white wine or clear spring water left in moonlight
white flowers such as jasmine or lilac
a spun or woven thread or a piece of weaving
a poem written under the stars
avoid: Don't try to trick or shame her; her myth is precisely about refusing to be controlled. Avoid taking shells or stones from protected beaches.
bestTime: Winter nights and clear summer nights when the Northern Crown is high (Jun–Aug); the winter solstice (Dec) in modern practice
caution: Most of her lunar and astral lore is modern; respect the Fourth Branch as Welsh literature and be clear about what is interpretation. A deity of fate and fierce independence is best approached with self-honesty.

name: Lugh
title: The Many-Skilled, Lugh of the Long Arm
pantheon: Irish (Gaelic Celtic), with Gaulish and Welsh cognates
represents: Lugh is the master of all arts: warrior, king, smith, harper, poet, physician, sorcerer and craftsman at once. He represents excellence, skill earned through practice, justice and oaths, leadership and the harvest bounty secured by labour. Modern pagans honour him as a bright god of the first harvest, of craftspeople, artists and anyone seeking to master their work.
description:
In Cath Maige Tuired, the young Lugh comes to the gate of Tara and is refused until he proves he holds every skill the court has a master of, and all of them together; he is admitted as Samildánach, 'skilled in many arts'. He is son of Cian of the Tuatha Dé Danann and Ethniu, daughter of the Fomorian tyrant Balor. Leading the Tuatha Dé in the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, he kills his grandfather Balor with a sling-stone through his destructive eye. His spear (the Spear of Lugh, one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé) and his title Lámhfhada, 'long arm', are famous. In the Ulster Cycle he is father of Cú Chulainn.

Lughnasadh (1 August) is said in medieval tradition to have been founded by Lugh in honour of his foster mother Tailtiu, who died clearing the plains of Ireland for agriculture; the Óenach Tailten games were held at Teltown, Co. Meath. Máire MacNeill's classic study The Festival of Lughnasa documents surviving harvest gatherings on hilltops, including the Reek Sunday pilgrimage on Croagh Patrick and Puck Fair in Killorglin.

Lugh is widely connected with the Gaulish god Lugus, whose name appears in place-names such as Lugdunum (Lyon), and with the Welsh Lleu Llaw Gyffes, though the precise relationships are debated. Julius Caesar's 'Mercury' of the Gauls, inventor of all arts, may refer to Lugus. Modern pagans celebrate Lughnasadh with loaf-baking, games, crafts and oath-making.
sacredDays: Lughnasadh (1 August), traditionally celebrated on hilltops on the last Sunday in July or first in August; Sundays.
howToInvoke: Bake or buy a fresh loaf and set it on a sunny altar with a gold or orange candle, a sheaf or vase of grain or sunflowers, and a tool of your own craft (a pen, brush, needle, hammer or instrument). Stand facing the sun or the east. Name the skills you are working to master and ask Lugh to sharpen your hand and mind. Share the bread: break off the first piece for him and eat the rest with thanks. Afterwards practise your craft for a while as an offering, and keep any oath you swore.
invocation:
Lugh of the long arm, Lugh of the shining spear,
master of every craft, come near, come near.
Harper and smith, poet and healer, king,
teach my hands the art of every good thing.
As the first loaf breaks and the golden grain is won,
let my work be true beneath the August sun.
Samildánach, many-skilled and bright,
I give my best to you, and walk in your light.
offerings: the first loaf of the harvest or homemade bread
fresh berries such as bilberries and blackberries
a finished piece of craftwork, art or music
games, races or friendly competition held in his honour
avoid: Avoid oath-breaking and sloppy, half-hearted work offered in his name; he values honesty and skill. Don't make offerings of stolen or wasted food.
bestTime: Lughnasadh and the first harvest (late Jul–Aug); also the start of any new job, craft or apprenticeship
caution: Lughnasadh customs are living Irish folk tradition; respect local festivals and pilgrimages. The Lugh/Lugus/Lleu identification is a scholarly theory, not settled fact.

name: Danu
title: Mother of the Tuatha Dé Danann
represents: Danu is honoured today as the primordial mother of the Irish gods, a goddess of the fertile land, flowing waters, ancestral wisdom and the deep sources of life. In practice she represents the nurturing earth, the bond with ancestors and land, and the abundance that flows from both. Her ancient form is mysterious, which leaves room for reverent, humble devotion.
description:
Danu is one of the most famous and least attested Irish deities. The nominative form 'Danu' never appears in medieval texts at all: it is a modern scholarly reconstruction from the genitive Danann in the name Tuatha Dé Danann ('peoples of the goddess Danu'). Some scholars argue the older name was simply Tuath Dé ('people of the god/gods'), with Danann added later by learned writers. The Lebor Gabála Érenn names a Danand, daughter of Delbáeth, mother of Brian, Iuchar and Iucharba, the 'three gods of Danann'.

Separately, Cormac's Glossary (c. 900) describes Anu as 'mater deorum hibernensium', the mother of the Irish gods, and connects her with the two breast-shaped hills of Dá Chích Anann, the Paps of Anu in Co. Kerry, and with prosperity in Munster. Whether Anu and Danand are the same goddess is debated. Popular claims linking her to the Danube, to a Hindu Danu, or to a vast pan-Celtic mother cult are speculative and not established.

No myths of Danu herself survive. Her central place in modern paganism, as Great Mother, river goddess and ancestress of the gods, comes from 19th- and 20th-century scholarship and from neopagan, Druid and goddess-spirituality writers. Many devotees honour her at the Paps of Anu, at rivers and wells, and in ancestral rites, with the understanding that their relationship is built more on intuition and land than on ancient texts.
items: a pair of stones or hills imagery
a cauldron or bowl of plenty
sacredDays: Modern practice: Beltane and Lughnasadh for fertility and harvest, Samhain for ancestors; any time spent at rivers, wells or sacred hills.
howToInvoke: Go to running water if you can, or set a bowl of water beside a green candle, seeds and a stone from your own land. Sit low on the earth and place your hands on the ground. Rather than demanding, introduce yourself and your ancestors, and acknowledge the land you live on and its peoples. Ask Danu for nourishment, ancestral wisdom or healing. Pour a little water, milk or mead back into the river or earth, give thanks, and spend a moment simply listening.
invocation:
Danu, deep mother, river and root,
from whom the gods themselves took shoot,
Anu of the twin green hills,
of the well that brims and the stream that spills,
I come as child of child of child,
of tilled field and of open wild.
Feed the seed and heal the land,
and hold my people in your hand.
offerings: fresh water or milk poured into the earth or a river
native trees planted on her behalf
avoid: Don't pour anything harmful (dyes, oils, salt, glitter) into rivers or wells, and don't claim invented myths as ancient lore.
bestTime: Beltane to Lughnasadh (May–Aug) for fertility and abundance; Samhain (Oct–Nov) for ancestral work
caution: Be especially honest here: almost nothing is known of an ancient Danu, and her modern Great Mother image is largely a reconstruction. The Paps of Anu are on private farmland and sacred to many; ask permission, follow the countryside code and leave nothing behind.

name: Hecate
title: Torchbearer of the Crossroads
represents: Hecate rules the in-between: crossroads, doorways, boundaries, the threshold of the underworld and the night. She bears torches through darkness, guides souls and seekers, holds keys to hidden places, and commands the restless dead and the powers of magic and herbcraft. She is protector of the household and its entry, of childbirth, and of travellers. Modern witches revere her as Queen of Witches and a guide in shadow work and personal transformation.
description:
Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE, lines 411-452) gives Hecate a remarkable hymn: daughter of the Titans Perses and Asteria, she is honoured by Zeus above all others and given a share in earth, sea and starry heaven, granting victory, wealth, success to fishermen and herders, and nurture to the young. In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter she hears Persephone's cries from her cave, meets Demeter with a torch in her hands, and afterward becomes Persephone's attendant and companion. Her oldest major cult centre was at Lagina in Caria (modern Turkey).

Athenians set small shrines called hekataia at doorways and crossroads, sometimes with three-faced images (the triple form is documented from the 5th century BCE onward, notably by the sculptor Alkamenes). At each new moon, the Hekate's Deipnon ('Hecate's supper') saw households clean their homes and leave food at the crossroads, often eaten by the poor. In later antiquity her role in magic grew enormously: Medea is her priestess in Apollonius' Argonautica, she is invoked across the Greek Magical Papyri, and the Chaldean Oracles make her a cosmic soul and saviour (Soteira). The Orphic Hymn to Hecate calls her saffron-robed, of the crossroads and tombs, and lover of solitude.

Ancient sources say dogs were sacrificed to her in some places; modern devotees do not do this, and her dogs are her companions rather than offerings. In modern witchcraft she is often cast as a Crone in the Maiden-Mother-Crone triad, an idea popularised by Robert Graves and not ancient: the ancient Hecate is usually depicted as a young woman. Today she is honoured by Hellenic polytheists, Wiccans and eclectic witches, with the monthly Deipnon among the most widespread devotional practices.
sacredDays: Hekate's Deipnon at each dark moon (the last day of the lunar month); the 13th of the month and 16 November ('Night of Hecate') in modern practice, and Samhain.
howToInvoke: On the night of the dark moon, clean your home thoroughly and sweep the dust out the door. Set two candles (as torches) and a key on a black cloth near your front door or at a safe three-way crossroads. Approach in silence, with your back straight, and call her by her epithets: Hecate Phosphoros, Kleidouchos, Soteira. Offer a small plate of food and ask her to guard your threshold, guide your decisions or open the way through a dark time. Leave the food at a crossroads or compost it, and walk home without looking back, a traditional gesture of respect.
invocation:
Hecate of the threefold road,
who lifts the torches, bears the load,
Key-holder, Saviour, Queen of night,
Light-bringer in the blackest sight,
guard my door and guide my feet
where the three ways cross and meet.
Take this supper, hear my plea,
and as I will, so let it be.
offerings: a Deipnon plate: bread, eggs, honey cakes, cheese, garlic, leeks
honey and fruit such as pomegranate
red or white wine or honeyed water
a thorough house cleansing done in her name
donations to animal shelters or food banks (following the Deipnon's feeding of the poor)
caring for stray or rescued dogs
avoid: Never sacrifice or harm animals. Traditionally offerings left at the crossroads were not taken back or eaten by the offerer; don't leave non-biodegradable items or litter, and don't block real roads.
bestTime: Late autumn through winter, especially Samhain to midwinter (Oct–Dec); every dark moon throughout the year
caution: Hecate is honoured in living Hellenic polytheism; respect its customs (e.g. purification before approaching). Be mindful that many sacred plants associated with her in lore (yew, poppy, and nightshades such as belladonna and aconite) are poisonous; use them only symbolically. She is a powerful goddess, not a vending machine.

name: Persephone
title: Queen of the Underworld and Maiden of Spring
represents: Persephone is the Maiden (Kore) who gathers flowers in the meadow and the dread Queen who rules the dead beside Hades. She embodies the cycle of descent and return, the seed below the ground and the green shoot above it, initiation, and the transformation of the innocent into the sovereign. Modern witches call on her for shadow work, journeys through grief or trauma, mediumship, and spring renewal.
description:
The fullest ancient account is the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (c. 7th-6th century BCE). While picking flowers, the maiden is seized by Hades, with Zeus's consent, as she reaches for a wondrous narcissus. Her mother Demeter searches for her with torches and, grieving, withholds the growth of crops until the world is starving. Zeus sends Hermes to fetch her back, but Hades gives her a pomegranate seed to eat, binding her to spend part of each year below. Her return each spring is celebrated as the return of life.

Persephone and Demeter were the central deities of the Eleusinian Mysteries, one of the most important religious rites of the ancient world, celebrated near Athens for perhaps a thousand years until suppressed in the late 4th century CE; initiates were sworn to secrecy and promised a better lot after death. She was also honoured at the women's festival of the Thesmophoria, and in Orphic tradition she is mother of Dionysus-Zagreus and the queen to whom initiated souls appealed on the gold tablets buried with the dead. Homer and other poets present her as a fearsome, majestic ruler of the dead.

Modern interpretations sometimes portray her as a willing bride rather than an abducted girl; the ancient hymn is clear that she was taken against her will, though her later sovereignty as Queen is equally ancient. Today she is honoured by Hellenic polytheists and eclectic witches at the spring equinox and in autumn, and is beloved as a patron of survivors who reclaim their power.
sacredDays: The spring equinox (her return) and the autumn equinox (her descent) in modern practice; anciently the Eleusinian Mysteries (Boedromion, Sept–Oct) and the Thesmophoria (Pyanepsion, Oct–Nov).
howToInvoke: Split a pomegranate and set it on a cloth that is half dark and half green, with one black and one green or pink candle. Place spring flowers on one side and dried leaves or a stone on the other. Light the dark candle first, then the light one, honouring both her queenship and her springtime. Address her as Queen and as Kore, and ask her guidance through your own descent or to help something return to life. Eat a few seeds yourself only if you wish to bind yourself to working with her; otherwise leave them as offering. Close with thanks and bury the pomegranate in the garden.
invocation:
Persephone, maiden of the meadow bright,
Queen beneath the earth in iron night,
you who tasted the red seed and became
the one who walks below and wears the flame,
go with me down the dark and winding stair,
and lead me back to blossom and to air.
Lady of descent and of return,
teach me the wisdom only shadow learns.
offerings: spring flowers such as narcissus, violets and roses
supporting survivors of abuse or charities for them
avoid: Avoid romanticising her abduction in a way that minimises harm; respect her as Queen. Don't make casual, joking pacts with her involving the dead.
bestTime: Spring equinox (Mar) for her return; autumn equinox through Samhain (Sept–Oct) for her descent
caution: Hellenic polytheism is a living religion; approach respectfully. Underworld and mediumship work can bring up grief and trauma, so ground yourself afterwards and seek support where needed. Poppies are associated with her; use only culinary poppy seeds or images, never opium preparations.

name: Demeter
title: Mother of the Grain and Giver of Law
represents: Demeter is the goddess of grain, agriculture and the fertile cultivated earth, of the bread on the table and the laws of settled life (Thesmophoros, 'bringer of law'). She is the fierce, grieving mother who would starve the world to have her daughter back, and so she rules both abundance and its withholding, the bond of mother and child, and the mysteries of life and death encoded in the seed. Modern witches turn to her for prosperity, nourishment, gardening, parenting and grief.
description:
Hesiod's Theogony names Demeter as a daughter of Kronos and Rhea, and mother of Persephone by Zeus. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter tells how, grieving for her daughter, she wandered the earth with torches for nine days, then disguised herself as an old woman and served as nurse in the house of Keleos at Eleusis. Iambe's jokes made her laugh; she refused wine and drank the kykeon, a drink of barley, water and pennyroyal (now known to be toxic; do not recreate). When the queen interrupted her attempt to make the infant Demophon immortal by fire, she revealed her divinity and ordered a temple built at Eleusis.

She withheld the crops until Zeus returned Persephone, then restored fertility and taught her rites, the Eleusinian Mysteries, to the leaders of Eleusis. She also gave the art of agriculture to Triptolemos, who spread it across the world. Her worship was everywhere in the Greek world: the Thesmophoria was an autumn festival of married women, the Haloa a winter festival, and first fruits (aparchai) of the grain harvest were sent to Eleusis. The Orphic Hymn to Demeter (Eleusinian) calls her all-mother, nurse of youths and bringer of the harvest.

The Romans equated her with Ceres, whose festival was the Cerealia in April. In modern paganism Demeter is often the Mother in a triple-goddess framework and is honoured at Lammas and the autumn equinox (Mabon), festivals that are modern wheel-of-the-year names rather than Greek ones, while Hellenic polytheists keep reconstructed versions of the Thesmophoria and celebrate her at harvest.
sacredDays: Thesmophoria (autumn sowing, Oct–Nov), the Eleusinian Mysteries (Sept–Oct), Haloa (winter), Roman Cerealia (12–19 April); modern Lammas and the autumn equinox.
howToInvoke: Set a loaf of bread, a sheaf or bowl of grain, a bowl of honey, and seasonal fruit on a golden cloth, with a gold or green candle. Ground yourself by standing barefoot or touching soil. Speak to her as a mother and a queen, thanking her first for the food you have eaten this year before asking for abundance, nourishment or comfort in grief. Break the bread and share it with others if possible. Afterward give a portion back to the earth or garden and make a donation of food to someone in need.
invocation:
Demeter, golden mother of the field,
whose grief made barren what your love could yield,
Deo of the torches and the sheaf,
who walked the world in search, who knows of grief,
bless the seed and the hand that sows,
the bread that rises and the grain that grows.
From your full lap may plenty pour,
and none go hungry at my door.
offerings: a sheaf of wheat or barley
seasonal fruit and the first produce of your garden
food donated to a food bank in her name
avoid: Avoid wasting food, especially at her altar. Never recreate the ancient kykeon with pennyroyal, which is toxic. Don't take her abundance for granted: thanks should come first.
bestTime: Harvest season, Lammas to the autumn equinox and Thesmophoria (Aug–Nov); also spring sowing (Mar–Apr)
caution: Hellenic polytheism is a living religion; approach with respect. The Eleusinian rites were secret and are not truly known, so beware of anyone claiming to teach the 'original' Mysteries. Pennyroyal and poppy (from her lore) are unsafe to ingest; use only symbolically.

name: Artemis
title: Lady of Wild Things, the Far-Shooting Huntress
represents: Artemis is the virgin huntress of mountains and forests, mistress of animals (Potnia Theron), protector of girls, of young creatures and of women in childbirth. She is wild, self-possessed and swift to defend her boundaries. Associated with the moon in later antiquity, she represents independence, the untamed self, protection of the vulnerable and the sacredness of wilderness. Modern witches call on her for confidence, boundaries, healing, women's mysteries and nature magic.
description:
Artemis is the daughter of Zeus and Leto and twin of Apollo, born on Delos (or Ortygia). The Homeric Hymns (especially numbers 9 and 27) praise her as the 'loud-crying' huntress who delights in arrows and the hunt, and Callimachus' Hymn to Artemis (3rd century BCE) has her ask Zeus for eternal maidenhood, a bow, a band of nymphs and the mountains as her domain. Myths show her defending her boundaries fiercely: Actaeon, who saw her bathing, was turned into a stag and torn by his own hounds.

Her worship was among the most widespread in Greece. At Brauron near Athens, young girls served her as arktoi ('little bears') before marriage, and women dedicated clothing to her after childbirth. At Sparta she was Artemis Orthia; at Ephesus her great temple, one of the Seven Wonders, honoured a distinct local form of the goddess. She was invoked as Locheia, helper in childbirth, a role inherited from her mother's labour. The festival of Mounichia in spring honoured her with round cakes ringed with small torches (amphiphontes), shining like the full moon.

Her identification with the moon (and with Selene and Hecate) developed in classical and later antiquity, and the Romans equated her with Diana. Modern pagans revere her as a moon goddess, a patron of wildlife and of women, and as an icon of autonomy; Dianic Wicca centres a related figure. Hellenic polytheists continue her worship in reconstructed forms.
sacredDays: Mounichia (spring, full moon of Mounichion, Apr–May), the Brauronia (every four years), Elaphebolia (the deer festival, Mar–Apr); the 6th day of the lunar month (her birthday in Athenian reckoning); full moons in modern practice.
howToInvoke: Go into wild nature if you can, to a forest or hillside, or create an altar with a silver candle, a crescent moon, a bowl of spring water, wildflowers and a small bow or arrow image. Stand tall and speak with confidence; she honours self-possession. Ask her to protect you, a child, an animal or a wild place, or to help you hold your boundaries. Offer round cakes with tiny candles at the full moon. Afterwards thank her and do something concrete for wildlife or for a young person in your life.
invocation:
Artemis, swift lady of the silver bow,
who runs where the wild deer and the cold streams go,
Potnia of beasts, Locheia, moon-crowned maid,
keeper of the young and the unafraid,
let me be whole and walk my own wild way,
and guard what's mine by night as well as day.
Far-shooter, bright one, fierce and free,
lend your aim and your courage to me.
offerings: round honey cakes with small candles (amphiphontes)
fresh fruit, especially figs and apples
a lock of hair or a girdle dedicated at a life transition
donations to wildlife conservation or habitat restoration
protecting or mentoring girls and young people
avoid: Avoid hunting or harming animals in her name, disrespecting wild places, or violating anyone's privacy and consent; her myths take boundaries very seriously.
bestTime: Spring into early summer (Mar–May), when Mounichia and the Elaphebolia fell; any wilderness retreat
caution: Hellenic polytheism is a living religion; respect its practitioners. Distinguish the ancient goddess from modern lunar and Dianic interpretations. Wormwood and mugwort are not safe in pregnancy; use them only externally or as incense.

name: Aphrodite
title: Foam-Born Goddess of Love and Beauty
represents: Aphrodite is the golden goddess of love, desire, beauty and pleasure, of the joining that makes the world fertile and the sweetness that makes life worth living. She rules erotic and romantic love, but also social harmony (as Pandemos), the heavenly love of the soul (as Ourania), sailors and the sea, and the courage of the heart. Modern witches call on her for self-love, romance, beauty and glamour magic, healing body image, and reconciliation.
description:
There are two ancient births. In Hesiod's Theogony, Kronos casts the severed genitals of Ouranos into the sea; white foam (aphros) gathers around them, and from it the goddess rises, first at Kythera and then at Cyprus, attended by Eros and Himeros (Desire). In Homer's Iliad she is instead the daughter of Zeus and Dione. The Homeric Hymns to Aphrodite (5, 6 and 10) tell of her love for the Trojan shepherd Anchises, by whom she bore Aeneas, and of the Horai clothing her in gold when she came ashore at Cyprus. She was married to Hephaestus and loved by Ares and by the mortal Adonis.

Her greatest sanctuaries were at Paphos and Amathus on Cyprus, at Kythera, and at Corinth on the Acrocorinth. She was honoured with the Aphrodisia festival in many cities, and Athenian women mourned Adonis at the Adonia by planting quick-withering 'gardens of Adonis' on rooftops. She is closely related to Near Eastern goddesses such as Ishtar/Astarte, likely reaching Greece via Cyprus and Phoenician contacts. Sappho's prayer to her (Fragment 1) is one of the most famous devotional poems of antiquity, and the Orphic Hymn to Aphrodite calls her heavenly, laughter-loving and mother of necessity.

Ancient offerings to her included incense (especially frankincense), flowers, and sometimes doves; today devotees keep to bloodless offerings. In Rome she became Venus, mother of the Roman people through Aeneas, and the planet Venus still bears her name. Modern witches and Hellenic polytheists honour her through beauty, art, love magic, and acts of kindness and pleasure, and on Fridays (Venus-day).
sacredDays: Fridays; the 4th day of each lunar month (shared with Eros in Athenian reckoning); the Aphrodisia festivals; the spring and Beltane season in modern practice.
howToInvoke: Bathe or wash before approaching, perhaps with rose water, and dress in something that makes you feel beautiful. Set a pink or gold candle, a mirror, a seashell, a bowl of sea water or salt water, roses and a dish of honey or fruit. Burn frankincense or myrrh. Look into the mirror with tenderness, then speak to her warmly and joyfully; she is philommeides, 'laughter-loving'. Ask for love, self-love, harmony or beauty in your life, never to bend another person's will. Close with thanks, and share something sweet or a kindness with someone afterward.
invocation:
Aphrodite, risen from the white sea-foam,
golden one of Paphos, Kypris, come home,
laughter-loving lady of the dove and rose,
in whose bright wake the sweet desire flows,
open my heart to love, and let me be
as kind to my own face as the tide to the sea.
Bring love that's true and joy that's free;
Cytherea, I give my praise to thee.
offerings: perfume or a dab of scented oil on her altar
acts of kindness to lovers, friends and strangers
avoid: Never use her name in coercive love spells that override another person's free will. Avoid neglecting her in favour of only asking; she is said to punish those who scorn love (as with Hippolytus).
bestTime: Spring and early summer, Beltane to midsummer (Apr–Jun); every Friday
caution: Hellenic polytheism is a living religion; approach respectfully. Love magic is best aimed at your own heart and openness rather than at a named person. Patch-test perfumes and oils, and keep candles away from flowers and fabric.
